result: The authors developed a novel D-loop Mapping Assay (DMA) that uses non-denaturing bisulfite treatment to modify cytosines on the displaced strand of D-loops, followed by single-molecule real-time sequencing to detect D-loop footprints with near base-pair resolution. The assay demonstrates high strand-specificity (>30-100 fold difference between top and bottom strands), homology-specificity (footprints confined to homologous regions), and dependence on Rad51/ssDNA for D-loop formation. The method detects ~60% of D-loops visualized by gel electrophoresis and is applicable to various substrate types and donor configurations.
evaluation: Claims C4-C7, C55, C62-C77, and C93 collectively provide strong evidence for the successful development and validation of the DMA. Multiple layers of internal controls (C69, C74-C77) confirm specificity, strand-specificity is demonstrated across multiple substrates (C62-C68), and correlation with gel-based quantification (C71-C73) validates the method. The comprehensive experimental design with negative controls and multiple substrate types strongly supports this major methodological advance.

result: D-loops formed on supercoiled donors have lengths tightly regulated by the supercoiling density of the donor DNA, with average lengths of 259±93 nt (ds98-931), 231±60 nt (ds98-607), and 206±48 nt (ds98-197-78ss), consistent with the predicted maximum of ~210±50 bp based on ~20±5 negative supercoils in 3 kbp plasmids. A small fraction (5-10%) of longer footprints (>350 nt) likely arise from nicked/relaxed plasmids in the reaction, and minimal branch migration occurs during bisulfite treatment.
evaluation: Claims C56-C61 establish the theoretical basis for length restriction based on DNA topology, while C82-C92 provide experimental validation. The observed average lengths closely match predictions from supercoiling density calculations (C58-C59, C82-C83). The explanation for longer footprints is supported by gel evidence showing 5-10% nicked plasmids (C89) and stability data from prior work (C88). The conclusion of minimal branch migration (C91-C92) is well-supported by the predominance of expected-length footprints.

result: D-loops are enriched at the 3' end of homology regardless of donor topology (supercoiled or linear), substrate sequence, or presence of a 3'-flap. This enrichment is consistent with 5'-to-3' directional growth of Rad51 filaments and may also reflect activation of Rad54 motor activity by the 3'-OH branchpoint. The distribution pattern is independent of cytosine distribution (as long as %CG is not very low) and topological barriers.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79 and C99 demonstrate 3' enrichment across multiple experimental conditions, supported by visual footprint maps and quantitative distribution analysis. The consistency across different substrates (C100-C102), donor types (C167), and validation with prior work (C79, C164) strongly support this finding. The mechanistic interpretations (C80, C165, C166) are appropriately presented as inferences supported by citations, though C81 and C166 remain speculative.

result: D-loops formed on linear (topologically unrestricted) donors exhibit a broad range of lengths from ~100 nt to the maximum homology length, with no preferred length. Average D-loop lengths are ~390 nt for 900 nt homology substrates and decrease to ~320 nt (607 nt homology) and ~176 nt (197 nt homology). Approximately 5% of D-loops span nearly the entire homology region (up to 900 nt). Homology length defines the maximum observable D-loop length and influences the average length, while a 78 nt 3'-flap does not significantly alter D-loop length distribution.
evaluation: Claims C94-C114 provide comprehensive characterization of D-loops on linear donors with high strand-specificity (>100 fold, C96), correlation with gel-based assays (C97), and homology-specificity (C98). The broad length distribution (C103-C105) is well-documented across multiple substrates, and the relationship between homology length and D-loop length (C110-C114) is systematically demonstrated. The minimum length limitation (C106) is appropriately attributed to the peak threshold. Statistical comparisons between substrates (C108-C109) support the conclusions about sequence and 3'-flap effects.

result: Human RAD51 and RAD54 proteins form D-loops with similar positional distribution (3' enrichment) as yeast proteins, but with lower formation efficiency (3% vs ~20-30%) and shorter average lengths (320±140 nt vs 410 nt for linear donors). Only 21% of D-loops formed by human proteins exceed 400 nt compared to >40% with yeast proteins, suggesting human proteins are less efficient at forming longer D-loops under the tested conditions.
evaluation: Claims C120-C131 demonstrate successful application of DMA to human proteins with appropriate controls and comparisons to yeast proteins. The lower efficiency (C127) and shorter D-loop lengths (C123-C125) are consistently observed and quantified. The correlation between gel-based and DMA quantification (C130) validates the measurements. The mechanistic interpretations (C128-C129) are appropriately presented as speculative, acknowledging the potential role of accessory factors. This demonstrates the broad applicability of the method across species.

result: Optimization of bisulfite treatment conditions identified room temperature (RT) for 3 hours as optimal, balancing cytosine conversion efficiency with minimizing D-loop migration/dissolution and DNA breathing. Higher temperatures (37°C for 4 hr or 70°C) caused excessive DNA breathing and non-specific conversions, while RT conditions showed better D-loop recovery compared to other tested conditions.
evaluation: Claims C132-C137 systematically evaluate temperature and time conditions with appropriate experimental evidence. The observation of non-specific conversions at 37°C for 4 hr (C134) and knowledge of D-loop instability at elevated temperatures (C133, C135) support the choice of RT conditions. The comparative data (C136) demonstrating better recovery at RT for 3 hr provides empirical justification for the selected conditions. This optimization is essential for method validity.

result: The optimal peak threshold for D-loop detection is t40w50 (40% cytosine conversion in a window of 50 consecutive cytosines), which eliminates the majority of footprints from spontaneous DNA breathing while maintaining sensitivity. This threshold is below the measured bisulfite conversion efficiency of 58% and eliminates nearly all bottom-strand and non-homologous region footprints. Lower thresholds (t25) increase false positives from DNA breathing, while higher thresholds (t60w20) result in loss of genuine D-loop footprints. The threshold affects measured D-loop length but not positional distribution.
evaluation: Claims C138-C156 provide systematic optimization of peak-calling parameters with clear experimental evidence. The conversion efficiency measurement (C138-C139) establishes the upper bound for the threshold, while testing multiple threshold combinations (C141-C147) demonstrates the balance between sensitivity and specificity. The observation that t40w50 eliminates background while t60w20 loses genuine footprints (C147) supports the choice. The effects on length measurements (C151-C154) are appropriately characterized, and the lack of effect on distribution (C155-C156) is important for interpretation.

result: The DMA cannot detect multi-invasions where a single substrate invades multiple donor molecules, but can detect multiple D-loop footprints within a single donor molecule (~2-5% of cases). At lower thresholds (t25w20), dual footprints on bottom-strand reads may represent D-loop junctions where the bottom strand is single-stranded, potentially bound by RPA (requiring ~25 nt single-stranded regions).
evaluation: Claim C117 correctly identifies a limitation of the method. Claims C118-C119 report the observation of multiple footprints per read but acknowledge the interpretation is speculative. Claims C148-C150 describe bottom-strand dual footprints at low thresholds, but C149 explicitly states this is speculative and C150 is an inference based on RPA binding properties. The inability to distinguish between genuine junction signals and DNA breathing artifacts (as noted in the text) makes these observations uncertain. Additional validation would be needed to confirm the biological significance of these patterns.

result: Several mechanistic interpretations are proposed: (1) variation in D-loop length may reflect differential Rad51 filament lengths or Rad54 processivity; (2) 3' enrichment may indicate that the 3'-OH branchpoint better activates Rad54 motor activity or reflects higher physical flexibility at the 3' end; (3) longer footprints with supercoiled donors may result from nicked plasmids or branch migration; (4) poor human RAD51 D-loop formation may reflect RAD51 filament instability or need for accessory factors.
evaluation: Claims C163, C166, C81, C87, C128, and C129 are explicitly speculative interpretations of observed data. While these hypotheses are reasonable and consistent with the data, they lack direct experimental validation. C87 presents two alternative explanations without definitively distinguishing between them (though C88-C91 favor the nicked plasmid explanation). C128-C129 acknowledge uncertainty about the mechanism underlying poor human protein performance. These remain plausible hypotheses requiring future experimental validation.
